```{r}
# A function takes 1 or more inputs called arguments. They often return an output.

sqrt(9)

# The function is the sqrt(), the input (9) which is the argument and the output is the square root of the number.
```

```{r}
# This is the rounding function and can be rounded to the required significant figures.
round(3.14159)
```
```{r}
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
# The sequence function generates a sequence of numbers with the arguments being in order: form (first number). to (last number) and by (the increment).

print(seq(1, 10, 2))
print(seq(5, 15, 5))
```
```{r}
# The name of the arguments can be used when required.

print(seq(by = 2, from = 1, to = 10))
print(seq(by = 5, to = 15, from = 5))
```
```{r}
# This function repeats the value,x, for a specific number of times. The order of the arguments is rep(x,times).

print(rep(2, 5))
print(rep(x = 2, times = 5))
```
```{r}
print(rep(5, 7))
print(rep(x = 5, times = 7))
```
```{r}
# A variable associates a specific name with a specific value by using the operator <-.

# This can be through saying my_variable and make it equal to the value of 12. R internally will know that that my_variable is equal to 12 and can be checked by using print().

my_variable <- 12
print(my_variable)
```
```{r}
# The value of the variable can be changed and the last version of the variable will be used.

my_variable <- 12
my_variable <- 10
print(my_variable)
```
```{r}
# Variables should be one word, without spaces and without punctuation (except for _) so the following would not work:

# my-var (uses the -)

# Variables can not start with a number, eg 1var would not work

# Some words have specific meaning in R so they can not be used as variable names, eg can not use 'if' as a variable
```
```{r}
# There are 3 types of variables:

# 1. Numeric variables:

# All variables which are numbers can be classed as numeric, eg x=1

x <- 1
print(x)
x <- 4e-3
print(x)

# 2. Character (string) variables:

# A character variable consists of text.

x <- "Hello"
print(x)

x <- "I am a variable"
print(x)

# 3. Logical (boolean) variables:

# These variables can only be true or false.

x <- TRUE
print(x)

x <- FALSE
print(x)

# The type of variable being used can be identified by using the class() function.

x <- "hi there"
print(class(x))

x <- 1513871
print(class(x))

x <- FALSE
print(class(x))
```
```{r}
cell_ID_1 <- "CX1"
treated_1 <- TRUE
num_cells_before_1 <- 5415
num_cells_after_1 <- 1432

cell_ID_2 <- "CX2"
treated_2 <- FALSE
num_cells_before_2 <- 8123
```
